title: Transcontinental railroad
notes: Cited for: Pacific Railroad Act 1862; Union Pacific and Central Pacific routes; Promontory Summit, May 10, 1869; Chinese workers about 90 percent of the Central Pacific workforce.

title: About the Homestead Act (Homestead National Historical Park)
notes: Cited for: Lincoln signed the Homestead Act; 160 acres for a filing fee; who proved up (immigrants, landless farmers, single women, formerly enslaved people).

title: People and Bison
notes: Cited for: 30 to 60 million bison to fewer than 1,000 by the 1890s; railways, rifles and the hide market drove the Great Slaughter; the military directive to destroy bison.

title: Battle of the Little Bighorn
notes: Cited for: June 25, 1876; Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse; the January 1876 ultimatum; Custer and his command killed; the army then forced surrender.

title: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868)
notes: Cited for: the 1868 treaty recognized the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation; 1874 Custer expedition and gold; United States v. Sioux Nation (1980) and the refusal of payment.

title: Wounded Knee Massacre
notes: Cited for: the Ghost Dance amid hunger and a shrinking reservation; December 29, 1890; about 150 to 300 Lakota killed by the 7th Cavalry, almost half women and children.

title: Kill the Indian, and Save the Man
publisher: Pennsylvania Center for the Book, Penn State University Libraries
notes: Cited for: Pratt opened the Carlisle school in 1879; his phrase "kill the Indian in him, and save the man"; hair cut, dress changed, native languages restricted.

title: Zitkála-Šá (Red Bird / Gertrude Simmons Bonnin)
notes: Cited for: Yankton Dakota writer taken to a boarding school at 8; 1900 Atlantic Monthly essays; founded the National Council of American Indians in 1926.

title: Dawes Act (1887)
notes: Cited for: allotment of reservation land (a quarter section per head of family); surplus land sold to non-Native settlers; the assimilation goal.

title: The Dawes Act
notes: Cited for: Native land fell from about 138 million acres before the Dawes Act to about 48 million by 1934.

title: Federal Law and Indian Policy Overview
publisher: Bureau of Indian Affairs, US Department of the Interior
notes: Cited for: the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 ended allotment.

title: How Did the Gilded Age Get Its Name?
notes: Cited for: the era is named after the 1873 novel The Gilded Age by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner; gilded means thinly covered in gold.

title: Andrew Carnegie
notes: Cited for: family emigrated from Scotland to Pittsburgh in 1848; bobbin boy at 13; sold his company to J.P. Morgan for $480 million in 1901; the Gospel of Wealth (1889).

title: Robber Barons (Dictionary of American History)
notes: Cited for: Matthew Josephson's The Robber Barons (1934) and Allan Nevins's 1940 Rockefeller biography as the two poles of the historians' debate.

title: Homestead Strike
notes: Cited for: the 1892 Carnegie Steel dispute; 300 Pinkerton agents; three Pinkertons and seven strikers killed; the militia broke the strike.

title: Trade union
notes: Cited for: a union is an association of workers that seeks better pay and conditions through collective bargaining with employers.

title: Uprising of 20,000 (1909)
notes: Cited for: Clara Lemlich called for a general strike in November 1909; the shirtwaist strike of mostly young immigrant women; gains in wages and hours.

title: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
publisher: Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor
notes: Cited for: March 25, 1911; 146 workers died, mostly young immigrant women; locked doors and blocked exits; the Factory Investigating Commission and new laws; Frances Perkins.

title: Finding and Sharing Eastern European Voices
notes: Cited for: the first large wave from eastern Europe came with immigrants from southern Europe between 1880 and 1920.

title: A Century of Immigration, 1820-1924 (From Haven to Home)
notes: Cited for: between 1881 and 1924 over two and a half million eastern European Jews came to the US, driven by persecution and lack of opportunity.

title: Ellis Island: Overview and History
notes: Cited for: Ellis Island opened in 1892; more than 12 million immigrants by 1924; about 2 percent excluded, mostly for contagious disease.

title: Chinese Exclusion Act (1882)
notes: Cited for: the first major federal law to suspend immigration for a specific nationality, barring Chinese laborers.

title: Repeal of the Chinese Exclusion Act, 1943
publisher: Office of the Historian, US Department of State
notes: Cited for: Congress repealed the exclusion acts in 1943, when China was a wartime ally.

title: U.S. Immigration Station, Angel Island
notes: Cited for: opened January 21, 1910, the main western port of entry for Asian immigrants; hearings could take days to months or years; poems carved into the barrack walls.

title: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
notes: Cited for: Louisiana's 1890 Separate Car Act; Homer Plessy's 1892 test case; the 7 to 1 ruling for separate but equal; Harlan's dissent.

title: United States: Jim Crow legislation
notes: Cited for: poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses used to disfranchise Black voters.

title: Toward a "Temporary Farewell": Anti-Lynching Legislation
publisher: US House of Representatives, History, Art & Archives
notes: Cited for: from Mississippi in 1890 to Georgia in 1908, every former Confederate state moved to disfranchise Black voters.

title: Ida B. Wells
notes: Cited for: the 1892 Memphis lynching of Thomas Moss and two other grocers; her investigation; the mob that destroyed her newspaper; Southern Horrors; the NAACP.

title: The History of the Standard Oil Company
notes: Cited for: Tarbell's 1904 book, serialized in McClure's, exposed Standard Oil's tactics and railroad rebates.

title: The Jungle
notes: Cited for: Sinclair's 1906 exposé of Chicago's meatpacking plants and the 1906 Meat Inspection Act and Pure Food and Drug Act.

title: Boss Tweed
notes: Cited for: Tweed's Tammany ring plundered New York City of an estimated $30 million to $200 million; Nast's cartoons; conviction in 1873.

title: Hull-House
notes: Cited for: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Hull-House in Chicago in 1889, with services such as classes, childcare and job help for immigrant neighbors.

title: Woman Suffrage in the West
notes: Cited for: Wyoming Territory, December 10, 1869, first; women of the West first to have full voting rights; many Native American women were not citizens.

title: Carrie Chapman Catt's "Winning Plan"
notes: Cited for: Catt's 1916 plan combined promising state campaigns with lobbying for a federal amendment.

title: Alice Paul
notes: Cited for: the Silent Sentinels picketed the White House from January 1917; arrests; Paul jailed for seven months and led a hunger strike.

title: Tennessee and the 19th Amendment
notes: Cited for: on August 18, 1920, Tennessee became the 36th state to ratify; Harry Burn cast the deciding vote after a letter from his mother.

title: Who was excluded?: Women's Suffrage
notes: Cited for: Black women in the South met poll taxes, literacy tests and violence; Native American women were not considered citizens until 1924.

title: 1920 Overview
notes: Cited for: the 1920 census was the first in which most Americans lived in urban areas.
